## Where you start

*Cold Chain* works on your laptop, in your browser, at `localhost`. This lesson gets it onto other people's screens: phones, tablets, a link you can send to your PI.

## Fit any screen

Your game is 960 × 540 game pixels. The **Scale Manager** decides how that fits the window.

{{< snippet file="stopping-points/stopE/src/main.js" lines="19-22" >}}

| Mode | What happens | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| `NONE` | Exactly 960 × 540 CSS pixels, whatever the window | Embedding at a fixed size |
| `FIT` | As big as fits, same shape, bars where it doesn't | Most games, including this one |
| `ENVELOP` | Fills the window, same shape, edges cropped off | Backgrounds you don't mind losing |
| `RESIZE` | The game becomes the size of the window | Games that can show more or less world |

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`FIT` with `CENTER_BOTH` is the safe default: the game is never stretched or cropped, and your coordinates never change. The bars on the sides take the page's background colour, which is why `index.html` sets the body to the same dark blue as the game.

`RESIZE` is the most work: the camera sees a different amount of the world on every screen, and every HUD position has to be worked out from `this.scale.width`. Worth it for some games; not for a first one.
:::

## Turn it sideways

On a phone held upright, a 16:9 game is tiny. *Cold Chain*, like the Minus 80 Studios games, asks you to turn the phone instead, with plain CSS in `index.html`:

{{< snippet file="stopping-points/stopE/index.html" lines="20-38" lang="css" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`pointer: coarse` means "the main input is a finger", so a narrow desktop window doesn't get the message. The game keeps running underneath; it's just hidden.

Phaser can also tell you about orientation in code (`this.scale.on('orientationchange', ...)`), and lock it on Android in full screen. CSS is simpler and works everywhere.
:::

## Touch

Phaser's **pointer** events work the same for a mouse and a finger: `pointerdown`, `pointermove`, `pointerup`. For a second finger at the same time, ask for it in the config (`input: { activePointers: 2 }`).

A floating joystick: put a thumb down anywhere and drag.

{{< snippet file="stopping-points/stopE/src/input/TouchStick.js" class="TouchStick" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The joystick turns the finger's position into the same kind of direction vector as the arrow keys, with x and y between −1 and 1. So `Play` doesn't care where input comes from:

```js
this.stick = this.sys.game.device.input.touch ? new TouchStick(this) : null;
// in update(): keys first, then the stick
if (this.direction.lengthSq() > 0) this.direction.normalize();
else if (this.stick) this.direction.copy(this.stick.vector);
```

Two details make it pleasant: it appears wherever the thumb lands (no hunting for a fixed button), and a short drag means a slow walk, because the vector's length is how far you dragged.

To test touch on a laptop, open your browser's developer tools and turn on **device mode** (the phone icon). Phaser then sees a touch screen.
:::

## Remember things

`localStorage` keeps small bits of text in the browser, for this site, until the user clears it.

{{< snippet file="stopping-points/stopE/src/save.js" lines="1-24" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Three things to know:

- **It stores strings.** Numbers come back as text: `'14242'`, not `14242`. Convert with `Number()`. For objects, `JSON.stringify` on the way in and `JSON.parse` on the way out.
- **It can fail.** Private windows, full storage and some embedded pages throw errors. Wrap every call in `try`, and let the game work without it.
- **It's shared by everything on the same site.** Every game at `you.github.io` shares one `localStorage`. Prefix your keys with the game's name (`cold-chain:best-time`) so two games don't overwrite each other's saves.
:::

## Build

`npm run dev` serves your source files and rebuilds as you edit. For the real thing, **build**:

```bash
npm run build
```

```
vite v8.3.8 building client environment for production...
transforming...
✓ 16 modules transformed.
rendering chunks...
computing gzip size...
dist/index.html                    0.77 kB │ gzip:   0.49 kB
dist/assets/index-Bfzm-BbR.js  1,383.73 kB │ gzip: 362.83 kB

(!) Some chunks are larger than 500 kB after minification. Consider:
...
✓ built in 531ms
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`dist/` now holds everything: one HTML file, one JavaScript bundle with Phaser and your code, and a copy of `public/assets/`. Any web server can host it. Check the build before you deploy:

```bash
npm run preview
```

The bundle is about 1.4 MB (360 kB once the server compresses it), almost all of it Phaser. That's normal for a Phaser game, and it's what the warning is about: Vite suggests splitting big bundles, but for a game that needs Phaser before it can do anything, there's nothing to gain. You can ignore it, or silence it with `build: { chunkSizeWarningLimit: 2000 }` in `vite.config.js`.
:::

## Relative paths

{{< snippet file="stopping-points/stopE/vite.config.js" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
By default Vite writes paths from the root of the site (`/assets/index-....js`). GitHub Pages serves your game from a sub-folder (`you.github.io/cold-chain/`), so those paths point to the wrong place and the page is blank (exercise 10.3). `base: './'` makes every path relative to the page, so the game works from any folder.
:::

## Put it online

GitHub Pages hosts static sites for free. With an **Action**, GitHub builds and publishes your game on every push.

1. Put your game in its own GitHub repository.
2. In the repository: **Settings → Pages → Source: GitHub Actions**.
3. Add this file as `.github/workflows/deploy.yml`, and push.

```yaml
name: Deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 26
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: dist
  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
A minute later the game is at `https://<your-username>.github.io/<repository>/`. This course site is published the same way (`.github/workflows/publish.yml`).

`npm ci` installs exactly what's in `package-lock.json`, so the build on GitHub uses the same Phaser and Vite as your laptop. Commit `package-lock.json`; never commit `node_modules/` or `dist/`.
:::

## When it's slow

- **Measure first.** `game.loop.actualFps` in the console, or the **Performance** panel in the developer tools.
- **Don't create things every frame.** Make objects once and reuse them: `disableBody` and `enableBody` (lesson 4), pooled groups, one tween you pause and resume (lesson 9).
- **Fewer, bigger textures.** Many small images cost more than one atlas (lesson 5).
- **Turn off what you can't see.** `setVisible(false)` and `setActive(false)` on things off screen.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
*Cold Chain* is far too small to be slow, so measure on the slowest phone you can find, not your laptop. That's where problems show up.
:::

## Exercises

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 10.1: Build it — a mute key" .exercise #ex-10.1}
Make **M** switch the sound off and on, on the title screen and during play. The title screen should say whether sound is on. The setting should survive a reload.

[Answer](../answers/10-ship-answers.qmd#ex-10.1)
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 10.2: Predict it — strings" .exercise #ex-10.2}
What does each line give? Try them in the console.

```js
localStorage.setItem('best', 14242);
const best = localStorage.getItem('best');
typeof best;
best + 1000;
best < 20000;
```

[Answer](../answers/10-ship-answers.qmd#ex-10.2)
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 10.3: Spot the bug — blank on GitHub" .exercise #ex-10.3}
A labmate's game works with `npm run dev` and `npm run preview`. On GitHub Pages, at `https://them.github.io/their-game/`, the page is blank, and the console shows a 404 for `https://them.github.io/assets/index-Bq3x9Lk2.js`. Their `vite.config.js`:

```js
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
export default defineConfig({});
```

[Answer](../answers/10-ship-answers.qmd#ex-10.3)
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 10.4: Tune it — thumb room" .exercise #ex-10.4}
In device mode (or on a real phone), try the joystick with a radius of 30, 56 and 110. Which is easiest to control, and why does a bigger radius feel slower?

[Answer](../answers/10-ship-answers.qmd#ex-10.4)
:::

## Key points

- `Scale.FIT` with `CENTER_BOTH` fits any screen without stretching. Ask phones to turn sideways with CSS.
- Pointer events cover mouse and touch. Turn a thumb into the same direction vector as the keys.
- `localStorage` stores strings, can fail, and is shared across a site: convert, `try`, and prefix your keys.
- `npm run build` makes `dist/`. Use `base: './'` so it works from any folder.
- A GitHub Action can build and publish your game on every push.

**Next:** your [capstone](../practice/capstone.qmd), and the [field guide](../field-guide/index.qmd) to *Snail Assassin*.
